{{short description|Trigonometric functions introduced by Indian mathematicians and astronomers}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:{{tlit|sa|Jyā}}, {{tlit|sa|koti-jyā}} and {{tlit|sa|utkrama-jyā}}}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2019}}
{{Use Indian English|date=August 2019}}
'''{{tlit|sa|Jyā}}''', '''{{tlit|sa|koṭi-jyā}}''' and  '''{{tlit|sa|utkrama-jyā}}''' are three [[trigonometric functions]] introduced  by [[Indian mathematics|Indian mathematician]]s and astronomers. The earliest known Indian treatise containing references to these functions is [[Surya Siddhanta]].<ref name="Datta">{{cite journal|last=B.B. Datta and A.N. Singh|date=1983|title=Hindu Trigonometry|journal=Indian Journal of History of Science|volume=18|issue=1|pages=39&ndash;108|url=https://linux.ime.usp.br/~bedulli/Datta-Singh_hindu-trigonometry-1983.pdf|access-date=2 June 2022}}</ref> These are functions of arcs of circles and not functions of angles. {{tlit|sa|Jyā}} and {{tlit|sa|koti-jyā}} are closely related to the modern [[trigonometric functions]] of [[sine]] and [[cosine]]. In fact, the origins of the modern terms of "sine" and "cosine" have been  traced back to the [[Sanskrit]] words {{tlit|sa|jyā}} and {{tlit|sa|koti-jyā}}.<ref name="Datta"/>

==Definition==
[[File:Modern diagram for jya and kojya.svg|thumb|right|250px|Modern diagram for {{tlit|sa|jyā}} and {{tlit|sa|kojyā}}]]

Let '{{math|arc AB}}'  denote an [[Arc (geometry)|arc]] whose two extremities are {{math|A}} and {{math|B}} of a circle  with center {{math|O}}. If a perpendicular {{math|BM}} is dropped from {{math|B}} to {{math|OA}}, then:

* {{tlit|sa|jyā}} of {{math|1=arc AB  = BM}}
* {{tlit|sa|koti-jyā}} of {{math|1=arc AB  = OM}}
* {{tlit|sa|utkrama-jyā}} of {{math|1=arc AB = MA}}

If the radius of the circle is {{mvar|R}} and the length of {{math|arc AB}} is {{mvar|s}}, the angle subtended by {{math|arc AB}} at {{math|O}} measured in radians is {{math|1=''θ'' =  ''s'' / ''R''}}. The three Indian functions are related to modern trigonometric functions as follows:

* {{math|1={{tlit|sa|jyā}} ( arc AB ) = ''R'' sin ( ''s'' / ''R'' )}}
* {{math|1={{tlit|sa|koti-jyā}} ( arc AB ) = ''R'' cos ( ''s'' / ''R'' )}}
* {{math|1={{tlit|sa|utkrama-jyā}} ( arc AB ) = ''R'' ( 1 − cos ( ''s'' / ''R'' ) ) = ''R'' [[Versine|versin]] ( ''s'' / ''R'' )}}

==<span class="anchor" id="Rsin"></span><span class="anchor" id="Rcos"></span>Terminology==
[[File:Jya and ardhajya.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Literal meaning of {{tlit|sa|jyā}}]]
[[File:Jya and kotijya.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Technical meaning of {{tlit|sa|jyā}} and {{tlit|sa|kojyā}}]]

An arc of a circle is like a bow and so is called a {{tlit|sa|dhanu}} or {{tlit|sa|chāpa}} which in [[Sanskrit]] means "a bow". 
The straight line joining the two extremities of an arc of a circle is like the string of a bow and this line is a chord of the circle. This chord is called a {{tlit|sa|jyā}} which in [[Sanskrit]] means "a bow-string", presumably  translating [[Hipparchus]]'s {{lang|grc|[[chord (geometry)|χορδή]]}}  with the same meaning{{citation needed|date=March 2017}}. 
The word {{tlit|sa|jīvá}} is also used as a synonym for {{tlit|sa|jyā}} in geometrical literature.<ref>According  to lexicographers, it is a synonym also meaning "bow-string", but only its 
geometrical meaning is attested in literature.  Monier-Williams, ''A Sanskrit Dictionary'' (1899): "'' jīvá''	n. (in geom. = ''jyā'') the chord of an arc; the sine of an arc ''Suryasiddhanta'' 2.57"; 
''jīvá'' as a generic adjective has the meaning of "living, alive" ([[:wikt:Appendix:Proto-Indo-European/gʷih₃wós|cognate]] with English ''[[:wikt:quick|quick]]'')</ref>
At some point,  Indian astronomers and mathematicians realised that computations would be  more convenient if one used the halves of the chords instead of the full chords and associated the half-chords with the halves of the arcs.<ref name="Datta"/><ref name="Glen">{{cite book|last=Glen Van Brummelen|title=The mathematics of the heavens and the earth : the early history of trigonometry|publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]|date=2009|pages=95&ndash;97|isbn=978-0-691-12973-0}}</ref> The half-chords were called {{tlit|sa|ardha-jyā}}s or {{tlit|sa|jyā-ardha}}s. These terms were again shortened to {{tlit|sa|jyā}} by omitting the qualifier {{tlit|sa|ardha}} which meant "half of".

The Sanskrit word {{tlit|sa|koṭi}} has the meaning of "point, cusp", and specifically "the [[Recurve bow|curved end of a bow]]".
In trigonometry, it came to denote "the complement of an arc to {{math|90°}}". Thus 
{{tlit|sa|koṭi-jyā}} is  "the {{tlit|sa|jyā}} of the complementary arc". In Indian treatises, especially in commentaries, {{tlit|sa|koṭi-jyā}} is often abbreviated as {{tlit|sa|kojyā}}. The term {{tlit|sa|koṭi}} also denotes "the side of a right angled triangle". Thus {{tlit|sa|koṭi-jyā}} could also mean the other [[cathetus]] of a right triangle, the first cathetus being the {{tlit|sa|jyā}}.{{clarify|date=October 2014}}<ref name="Datta"/>

{{tlit|sa|Utkrama}} means "inverted", thus {{tlit|sa|utkrama-jyā}} means "inverted chord". 
The tabular values of {{tlit|sa|utkrama-jyā}} are derived from the tabular values of {{tlit|sa|jyā}} by subtracting the elements from the radius in the reversed order.{{clarify|date=October 2014}} This is really{{clarify|date=October 2014}} the arrow between the bow and the bow-string and hence it has also  been called {{tlit|sa|bāṇa}}, {{tlit|sa|iṣu}} or {{tlit|sa|śara}} all meaning "arrow".<ref name="Datta"/>

An arc of a circle which subtends an angle of {{math|90°}} at the center is called a {{tlit|sa|vritta-pāda}} (a quadrat of a circle). Each zodiacal sign defines an arc of {{math|30°}} and three consecutive zodiacal signs defines a {{tlit|sa|vritta-pāda}}. The {{tlit|sa|jyā}} of a {{tlit|sa|vritta-pāda}} is the radius of the circle. The Indian astronomers coined the term {{tlit|sa|tri-jyā}} to denote the radius of the base circle, the term {{tlit|sa|tri-jyā}} being indicative of "the {{tlit|sa|jyā}} of three signs". The radius is also called {{tlit|sa|vyāsārdha}}, {{tlit|sa|viṣkambhārdha}}, {{tlit|sa|vistarārdha}}, etc., all meaning "semi-diameter".<ref name="Datta"/>
 
According to one convention,  the functions {{tlit|sa|jyā}} and {{tlit|sa|koti-jyā}} are respectively denoted by "Rsin" and "Rcos" treated as single words.<ref name="Datta"/> Others denote {{tlit|sa|jyā}} and {{tlit|sa|koti-jyā}} respectively by "Sin" and "Cos" (the first letters being capital letters in contradistinction to the first letters being small letters in ordinary sine and cosine functions).<ref name="Glen"/>

==From jyā to sine==
{{main|Sine and cosine#Etymology}}
The origins of the modern term sine have been traced to the Sanskrit word {{lang|sa|jyā}},<ref>{{cite web|url=http://mathforum.org/library/drmath/view/54053.html|title=How the Trig Functions Got their Names|work=Ask Dr. Math|publisher=[[Drexel University]]|access-date=2 March 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Trigonometric_functions.html |title=The trigonometric functions|last= J J O'Connor and E F Robertson|date=June 1996 |access-date=2 March 2010}}</ref>  
or more specifically to its synonym {{lang|sa|jīvá}}.
This term was [[Indian influence on Islamic science|adopted in medieval Islamic mathematics]], transliterated in Arabic as {{Transliteration|ar|jība}} ([[:wikt:جيب|{{lang|ar|جيب|cat=no}}]]). Since Arabic is written without short vowels – and as a borrowing the long vowel is here denoted with {{Transliteration|ar|yāʾ}} – this was interpreted as the [[homograph]] {{Transliteration|ar|jaib}}, {{Transliteration|ar|jayb}} ([[:wikt:جيب|{{lang|ar|جيب|cat=no}}]]), which means "bosom". The text's 12th-century  [[Medieval Latin|Latin]] translator used the Latin equivalent for "bosom", [[wikt:sinus|{{lang|la|sinus|cat=no}}]].<ref>Various sources credit the first use of {{lang|la|sinus}} to either: 
* [[Plato Tiburtinus]]'s 1116 translation of the ''Astronomy'' of [[Al-Battani]]
* [[Gerard of Cremona]]'s c. 1150 translation of the ''Algebra'' of [[Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī|al-Khwārizmī]]
* [[Robert of Chester]]'s 1145 translation of the tables of al-Khwārizmī
See Merlet, [https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/1-4020-2204-2_16#page-1 ''A Note on the History of the Trigonometric Functions''] in Ceccarelli (ed.), ''International Symposium on History of Machines and Mechanisms'', Springer, 2004<br>See Maor (1998), chapter 3, for an earlier etymology crediting Gerard.<br>See {{cite book |last=Katx |first=Victor |date=July 2008 |title=A history of mathematics |edition=3rd |location=Boston |publisher=Pearson |page=210 (sidebar) |isbn= 978-0321387004 |language=en }}</ref>  When {{lang|sa|jyā}} became {{lang|la|sinus}}, it has been suggested that by analogy {{lang|sa|kojyā}} became {{lang|la|co-sinus}}. However, in early medieval texts, the cosine is called the {{lang|la|complementi sinus}} "sine of the complement", suggesting the similarity to {{lang|sa|kojyā}} is coincidental.<ref>{{cite web|title=cosine|url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/cosine}}</ref>
